newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks choppy, lower after Intel-led sell-off.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks choppy, lower after Intel-led sell-off.

text.p: U.S. stocks were lower at midday Friday in choppy trading after recovering somewhat from a steep morning sell-off sparked by Intel Corp's warning of weaker-than-expected second-quarter profits.
The Dow Jones industrial average was down about 45 points, or 0.62 percent, at 7284, halving its losses since touching a low of 7242, down 88 points.
The Nasdaq composite index was also soft, down 20 at 1383. It had fallen about 47 points at the opening.
The long bond was up 19/32 to yield 6.93 percent.

Earlier, Intel, the world's largest computer chipmaker, said it expected second-quarter revenues to drop five to 10 percent from last quarter's $6.4 billion. It said profits would fall short of industry analysts' forecasts.
The news stunned Wall Street, especially because Intel has consistently managed to beat forecasts in the past.
"Growth or momentum investors are programmed to sell at the first hint of disappointment -- and they did. Intel is a bellwether stock in one of the fastest-growing industries," one analyst said.
At midday, Intel was off 13-41/64 to 150-1/8, with more than 38 million shares traded, after tumbling as low as 137-7/8.

With only about half the trading session over, Intel stands in 12th place for the greatest volume by any individual issue in a single session. That record is held by Comparator Systems Corp. Some 177.7 million Comparator shares changed hands on May 7, 1996, according to the Nasdaq.
One trader said stocks recovered as investors took a closer look at Intel's forecast of gross margins of 60 percent instead of 64 percent, which was not seen as drastic change.
"That's just a tempest in a teapot," he said.
Once investors got over their initial scare, bargain hunters moved in, analysts said.

Some Wall Street analysts also took comfort in the fact that Intel's warning provided evidence of a gradual slowing in the U.S. economy, which could suggest no need for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates soon.

"This backs up (Fed chairman) Alan Greenspan's decision not to raise rates. The economy is slowing and there have to be some disappointments in the business cycle," said Chris Dickerson, analyst at Global Market Strategists Inc.
The brightened outlook for rates, and a move by the bond yield back below seven percent, sent bank stocks surging. A key banking index .BKX rose nine to 601, up 1.5 percent.
Chase Manhattan Corp rose 1-5/8 to 94-1/2. Citicorp rose 3-3/4 to 113-3/8. J.P. Morgan & Co was up 1-7/8 to 106-1/4.

Compaq Computer Corp defied the general malaise with a rise of 3 to 104-7/8. Its chief executive said Compaq expected to meet second-quarter earnings estimates and said the world's largest personal computer maker was having none of Intel's difficulties in Europe.
Sunglass Hut International Inc shares were 7/8 lower at 6-3/4 after its president and chief executive resigned and the retailer said its sales remained sluggish in May.
